common_name: Red Bartlett Pear (Red-Skinned Sport of Classic Bartlett)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Red Bartlett requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Red Bartlett is a naturally occurring red-skinned sport of the classic green Bartlett pear, discovered as a bud mutation and propagated for its striking burgundy-red skin, while retaining the same sweet, juicy, melting flesh and classic pear flavor that made Bartlett the standard American pear for over a century. Because the tree and fruit share Bartlett's genetics apart from skin color, growers get the familiar reliable flavor with added ornamental interest in the orchard and a more eye-catching fruit for fresh eating, gift baskets, and market sales. Harvest while still firm and green-tinged with a hint of red blush, then finish ripening at room temperature indoors, since pears ripen from the inside out and develop the best texture and flavor off the tree rather than fully ripened on the branch.

common_name: Red Anjou Pear (Red-Skinned Firm Winter Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Red Anjou requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is best adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Red Anjou is a red-skinned bud sport of the classic D'Anjou pear, carrying the same dense, firm, sweet, low-fiber flesh and outstanding storage life as the parent variety, wrapped in a deep burgundy-red skin that adds visual appeal without altering flavor or texture. Like other Anjou-type pears, the fruit does not change color noticeably as it ripens, which makes checking for ripeness by color unreliable — instead, press gently near the stem end and harvest or eat once that area yields slightly to pressure. Anjou-type pears are prized for exceptionally good long-term cold storage, often holding good quality for months, making Red Anjou a satisfying choice for home orchardists who want fresh pears well into winter.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Summercrisp requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is exceptionally cold-hardy, well adapted to zones 3-7.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Summercrisp was bred by the University of Minnesota for extreme cold hardiness and good resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that devastates many European pears, making it a reliable choice for northern growers who struggle with more tender pear varieties. Unlike most European pears, which must be picked hard and ripened off the tree, Summercrisp is meant to be eaten while still firm and crisp, straight off the tree or shortly after picking, with sweet, juicy flesh and a flavor reminiscent of a crisp Asian pear crossed with a European one. Fruit ripens early, in mid to late summer well ahead of most storage pears, giving northern growers a reliable pear harvest even in regions where longer-season varieties may not fully mature.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Luscious requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is exceptionally cold-hardy, well adapted to zones 3-7.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Luscious was bred by South Dakota State University specifically for the harsh northern Great Plains climate, combining excellent cold hardiness and good fire blight resistance with genuinely good eating quality, living up to its name with sweet, juicy, melting flesh comparable to much less hardy European dessert pears. The medium-sized, greenish-yellow fruit ripens in early to mid fall and should be picked while still firm, then ripened at room temperature indoors for the best texture, as with most European-type pears. Its combination of hardiness and flavor has made it a favorite recommendation for northern home orchardists who want a genuinely good fresh-eating pear without relying on tender varieties bred for milder climates.

common_name: Golden Spice Pear (Cold-Hardy Canning and Preserving Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Golden Spice requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is exceptionally cold-hardy, well adapted to zones 3-7.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Golden Spice was bred in Minnesota for extreme cold hardiness and reliable production even in short northern growing seasons, producing small to medium, yellow-skinned pears with a distinctively spicy-sweet flavor that makes them outstanding for canning, spiced preserves, and pear butter, more than for out-of-hand fresh eating. The tree is notably productive and resistant to fire blight, bearing heavily and consistently once established, which has made it a long-standing favorite among northern home orchardists focused on putting up preserves rather than fresh market fruit. Harvest while still firm in early to mid fall and process promptly, or ripen briefly at room temperature if fresh eating is preferred, keeping in mind that the flavor truly shines once cooked with sugar and spice.
